name: Carla Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing economics, and I live in a flat on Quay Road with two friends from my course. A normal week is lectures, problem sets, and then lots of hours on my cake-topper business, where I design custom toppers and sell them online. I use AI all day, for designs, captions, maths help, planning, everything. At the weekend I go home to Portwell, where my family has four bakeries, and help with the Saturday rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because I'm already getting a lot out of it as it is. It saves me hours, and that's enough for me. At home we'd say bread still needs to be baked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I stay on my path: finish economics, build my topper business, help my parents with the bakeries. My dad Joaquim says it every time. Nobody has ever stopped eating cake because of a new technology. I think he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building the business, maybe add a second product, like custom cookie boxes. I'd keep up my studies and my weekend shifts. I'd also take a short small-business course to learn the numbers properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like it when things are stable, so I can build. My parents pay my costs, and the bakeries are doing fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a second product need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A design, a supplier and a price. I'd use the AI to make ten designs in an afternoon, then ask customers which they like. Mum Ines says the shoppers always tell you the truth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the bakeries use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. We use it for ordering and for scheduling the staff. Dad was sceptical, but he's pleased with the staff rota. It took ten minutes instead of two hours.

At home we'd say bread still needs baking.

Nobody stops eating **cake** because of new technology.

feel: **Calm**, because stable times let me build.

fieldNote: Uses AI for **design and testing**, and checks with real customers.

steps.text: Launch custom cookie boxes as a second product
Take a short small-business accounting course
Keep working Saturday rushes at the family bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who work, and a risk for people who wait for someone to fix things. I'd say free markets will sort it, if government doesn't get in the way. And I'd say it with a smile and a post on my business page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my economics degree is useful, but the business is what really counts. A lot of jobs like writing and planning will go, but cakes and bakeries need real hands. I'm in a good position with both. My friends who are going into marketing seem more nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a lot more AI into my business: designs, ordering, customer replies. I'd also help the bakeries use it for stock and rotas, and I'd propose to Dad that we open an online order option. I'd keep the degree, because it teaches me how markets move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous for friends. I'm the sort who'd rather act than worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would your family bakery need online orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People want to order a birthday cake at midnight. That's when they think of it. If we don't take the order, a supermarket will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends are nervous?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, who's doing communications. She's good, but she's seeing job ads vanish. I told her to start a side project, because the sooner she builds something, the sooner she knows what she's worth.

I'd say free markets will sort it.

Propose **online orders** to Dad for all four family bakeries.
feel: **Excited**, a bit nervous for friends, and happier acting than worrying.

steps.text: Add AI to designs, ordering and customer replies in the topper business

Keep learning new AI design tools every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and fast, but I'd say don't freeze. People who build and own will survive. I'd say we should keep markets open, and I'd say families should hold together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared, but I'd also think the hands-on side is safer for three more years. Our bakeries have staff, ovens and recipes; the AI would do the orders and accounts, but someone still bakes. My economics degree would be a lot less useful, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into the family bakeries and my business. I'd talk to Dad about turning the bakeries into a stronger, more automated chain. I'd reduce my study load or even pause the degree, because the real learning would be in the shops. I'd save what I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but active. It would keep me up, and then I'd be up doing something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really pause the degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was pointless, yes. I'd rather learn on the job, because by 2031 the family business is the thing that holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robot bakers would come eventually. But if my family owned the shops and the robots, we'd be fine. I'd want to own the robots, not be replaced by them.

say: I'd say it's **huge and fast**, but people shouldn't freeze.
I'd say people who build and own will survive.
think: The **hands-on** side of the bakeries gets three more years, but my degree matters less.
do: Throw myself into the **bakeries** and talk to Dad about a stronger, automated chain.
Reduce my study load or **pause the degree**.
feel: **Anxious**, but active, and up doing something about it.
S2.quote: I'd want to own the robots, not be replaced by them.
fieldNote: Her instinct is **ownership**, which fits her traditional, pro-market view.
Treats the family bakery as a lifeboat.
Willing to pause her degree if it has no value.

steps.text: Work with Dad to automate orders and accounts across the four bakeries
Put profits from the topper business into the family bakeries
Reduce my study load and consider pausing the degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get ready and anyone who uses it well will do fine. I'd say start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little anxious but mostly optimistic. I'd graduate in 2029 and have two years before AGI, which is enough to build a real business. I'd want to be an owner by then, not an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, keep growing the topper business, and work with my family to build an online ordering system. I'd put some profit into new equipment for the bakery. I'd also save in a boring account, as my mum suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. It feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better oven and a packaging machine for the cookie boxes. They save labour, and that cuts costs in a world where prices may drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does ownership matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if everything else is done by AI, whoever owns the stuff gets the money. I'd rather be the person who owns it than the person who's grateful for a wage.

say: I'd say five years is **long enough** to get ready if people use it well.
think: I'd have **two years** after graduating to build a real business.
I want to be an **owner**, not an employee.
do: Finish the degree, grow the topper business and build **online ordering** with my family.
Put profit into new **bakery equipment** and save in a boring account.
feel: **Anxious**, but motivated, like a race I can win.
S3.quote: If everything else is done by AI, whoever owns the stuff gets the money.
fieldNote: Ownership logic is the **core** of her plan.
Balances risk with a boring savings account on her mum's advice.

steps.text: Buy a better oven and a packaging machine for the bakeries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and there's lots we can build. I'd say it's an exciting time to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm confident. I'd be 28, with a business and maybe a family. I'd have years of experience of working with AI, and a family business with solid roots. Ten years gives me room to fail and try again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, and then run a bakery chain's expansion or start my own food brand. I'd marry and settle in Portwell, because I want my children to know their grandparents. I'd save and invest steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and eager. It's the one that makes me happiest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about people who are afraid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show them, with something small. My gran Dolores uses a tablet now to order flour, and she was convinced she couldn't. Show people one useful thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The world being less fair. If a few firms own the tools, ordinary people have less say. I'd want rules that keep competition alive.

I'd say it's an exciting time to start.

feel: **Calm** and eager, because this is the picture that makes me happiest.
fieldNote: Optimism rests on **ownership and family roots**.
Her gran's tablet story shows how she thinks about helping others.

steps.text: Finish the degree and lead the bakery chain's expansion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years is too little for the family business to catch up, and my degree would lose most of its value. What would help is time, cheap tools for small firms, and rules that keep competition alive so a few firms don't own everything. And my family. We'd hold together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I sound confident, but a lot of that is that I've seen small businesses survive. I'd want the same chance for everyone, not just families like mine.

headlineQuote: I sound confident, but a lot of that is that I've seen small businesses survive.
portrait: Carla is an **economics student** who sells custom cake toppers and helps at her family's four bakeries.
She uses AI **every day** and has already brought it into the bakeries' ordering and rotas.
Traditional and pro-market, she thinks in terms of **ownership**: own the shops and the machines.
Her mood runs from calm at a plateau to **anxious** at 2028 and 2031, and calm at ten years.
She knows her **family cushion** helps and wants fair competition for others.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the family bakeries and her degree get no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, cheap tools for small firms, and rules that keep **competition** alive.
